title: Security
description: Tenant isolation, manage roles, rate limits, risky sign-ins, security emails, outbound calls, signing-key rotation, pushed and signed requests, DPoP, and rich authorization requests.
---

This page covers how masks keeps tenants apart, limits managers and attackers, tells actors about
changes, and hardens the requests apps send.

Two related subjects live on other pages:

- How masks encrypts secrets at rest: [self-hosting](/build/self-hosting/#encryption-and-secrets).
- How to block a device before it can try a password:
  [sessions and devices](/build/features/#sessions-and-devices).

## Tenant isolation

masks keeps each tenant's data apart in four ways:

- The app limits every query to the current tenant.
- Postgres row-level security filters every row by tenant, so a query the app forgets to limit
  still sees one tenant's rows.
- Each tenant signs tokens with its own keys. A token from one tenant fails verification in every
  other.
- Each tenant's encrypted columns use a key made from the primary key and the tenant's ID. A value
  moved into another tenant fails to decrypt.

Some database roles get around row-level security:

- A `SUPERUSER` or `BYPASSRLS` role skips every policy, with no error.
- The role that owns a table can switch its policy off with one `ALTER TABLE`.

So masks checks its database role the first time it enters a tenant:

- It refuses to run as a role that holds either privilege.
- Outside development and test, it also refuses a role that owns a table that row-level security
  protects. Engine mode skips this check.
- It refuses a connection pooler in transaction mode, which drops the tenant between one statement
  and the next. See [connection poolers](/build/self-hosting/#connection-poolers).

This is why the server migrates as one role and serves as another. See
[database roles](/build/self-hosting/#database-roles).

### Entering a tenant

masks enters a tenant before it runs any request or job.

- A request enters the tenant its hostname names. A hostname with no tenant gets a 404 (Not Found)
  response.
- A job enters the tenant it was enqueued in. A job enqueued outside a tenant raises an error. A
  job that works across every tenant must declare it:

  ```ruby
  class CleanupJob < ApplicationJob
    across_tenants!
  end
  ```

Other code that works across tenants uses `Tenant.switch(tenant) { ... }`. Outside a tenant, a query
on a tenant's table returns no rows.

## Manage roles

Each manager holds one or more of four scopes.

| Scope | Can |
| --- | --- |
| `masks:manage:read` | Read everything `/manage` shows, and download activity. Change nothing. |
| `masks:manage:support` | Read. Help actors: add, invite, and approve them, change their profiles, sign them out, suspend and restore them, reset passwords and second factors, and block their devices. Revoke their sessions, consents, and tokens. Change organization members. |
| `masks:manage:security` | Read. Change signing keys, clients, SAML applications, providers, sign-in policies, sending services, event streams, organizations, groups, namespaces, and domain claims. Issue provisioning tokens for one organization. |
| `masks:manage` | Everything. This includes tenant settings and branding, risky networks, email templates, LDAP, serving a custom domain, the key rotation schedule, deleting actors, and granting any scope. |

How masks checks a role:

- A token for `/manage` carries the scopes the actor holds and `/manage` asked for.
- On every request, masks uses only the roles that both the token and the actor still hold.
- Every mutation in the [manage API](/reference/manage/) needs one role. A mutation that names none
  needs `masks:manage`.
- For a manager below `masks:manage`, a line at the top of each page in `/manage` says what they can
  change.

Taking a role away takes effect on the actor's next request. When they hold no manage role at all,
masks refuses their token.

### Limits on the narrower roles

A role below `masks:manage` has these limits:

- **It cannot change another manager.** This includes a session, token, consent, connection, or
  device that belongs to a manager. So support cannot change a manager's email address and then
  reset their password.
- **It cannot take over anyone's account.** Three actions need both `masks:manage:support` and
  `masks:manage:security`, or `masks:manage`:
  - changing an actor's email address
  - generating their backup codes
  - receiving a password reset link when masks cannot email the actor

  Support can still send a reset link to the actor's own email address. It can also reset the
  actor's second factors.

- **It cannot give out manage access.** It cannot give an actor or a client any manage scope or
  `masks:scim`. It cannot issue a provisioning token for every account. Either one would reach
  managers through [SCIM](/build/sso-saml/#provisioning).
- **It cannot change a client that can carry a manage scope or `masks:scim`.** So it cannot point
  `/manage` at another address.
- **It cannot connect `/manage` in a new browser.** It can open `/manage` in a new browser once an
  owner has connected it.

## Rate limits

A rate limit counts attempts over a period of time. Once the count reaches the limit, masks refuses
more. An API answers with the HTTP status 429 (Too Many Requests). A page in the browser shows a
message.

Every limit is a named budget with a default. An operator sets one with its environment variable or
under `limits:` in `MASKS_CONFIG`. Each time a budget runs out, masks records one `limit.reached`
event for that budget, address, and window, so a flood shows up in the activity as one line. See
[rate limits](/reference/environment/#rate-limits) for every budget and its default.

These limits are fixed:

| Endpoint | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Token, pushed request, device authorization, and SAML sign-in and logout | 60 per IP address each minute |
| Introspection and revocation | 120 per IP address each minute |
| SCIM and received security events | 600 per IP address each minute |
| Enrollment, forward authentication, and `/metrics` | 30 per IP address each minute |
| Enrollment tokens | 60 per app each hour |
| Organization invitations | 30 per account each minute |
| Account download | 5 per account each hour |

## Risky sign-ins

masks can give each sign-in a risk score from 0 to 100. It does this when a sign-in policy sets a
score to act on. The score is worked out right after the first factor.

| Signal | Adds |
| --- | --- |
| A device the account has not signed in from in 90 days, or no device at all. A trusted device does not count. | 30 |
| A network the account has not signed in from in 90 days. For IPv4, a network is the addresses that share the first three numbers (a /24). For IPv6, it is a /48. | 25 |
| An address in one of the tenant's **Risky networks** | 50 |
| Three or more refused attempts on the account in the last hour. Ten or more adds 40 instead. | 20 |
| No sign-in for six months | 10 |
| A password found in a known breach | 40 |

An account with no sign-in in the last 90 days has nothing to compare, so the device and the network
add nothing.

To act on the score, use **Risk** in a sign-in policy:

- **Ask for a second factor at a score of** asks for a second factor from that score up. An account
  without one is asked to add one, as in [step-up](/build/enterprise/#step-up-authentication).
- **Refuse at** stops the sign-in from that score up, and asks for the first factor again. It must
  be higher than the score that asks for a second factor.

Any score above zero is recorded as `sign_in.risky`, with the signals, and the actor gets a security
email.

A manager holding `masks:manage` lists the tenant's risky networks under **Settings**, then
**Policies**, then **Who may sign in**.

### Breached passwords

**Refuse passwords found in known breaches** checks passwords against the
[Pwned Passwords](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#PwnedPasswords) range API. It checks each new
password an actor chooses, at signup, from an invitation, at a reset, or on the account page. It
also checks each password used to sign in.

The password never leaves the server:

1. masks takes the password's SHA-1 hash, a fixed-length code computed from the password.
2. It sends only the first five characters of the hash.
3. It compares the rest of the hash itself.

What masks does with the result:

- A new password that is breached is refused.
- A breached password used to sign in adds to the risk score.
- If the service does not answer within three seconds, or answers with an error, masks allows the
  password.

## Security emails

masks emails an actor when something changes on their account.

| Group | Sent when |
| --- | --- |
| Password | The password is changed or reset. |
| Factors | A passkey, an authenticator app, or email or SMS codes are added or removed. Backup codes are generated, or one is spent. The actor asks for help, or a manager resets their second factors. |
| Sessions | A new device signs in. A sign-in gets a risk score above zero. A session is signed out. A device is blocked. |
| Apps and connected accounts | An app is allowed in. A connected account is connected or removed. A device sign-in is approved. |
| Account | The phone number is changed or removed. A manager changes the actor's scopes. The actor downloads their account. |
| Organizations | Someone else changes the actor's role in an organization, or removes them. Someone archives an organization the actor is signed in to an app for. See [what members are told](/build/organizations/#what-members-are-told). |

- masks reports a new sign-in once per device.
- Emails go only to a confirmed address. An account with no confirmed address gets none, and the
  account page says so.
- An actor can turn an email off under **Emails we send you** on the account page. A changed
  password, a reset password, and a risky sign-in are always sent. Changing which emails arrive
  asks for a sign-in within the last 15 minutes, and the change is recorded in the account's
  activity as *Notifications changed*.
- When the email address changes, masks also warns the previous address. This warning goes out
  even if the old address was not confirmed or the actor turned the group off.
- Each email names the device and the IP address the change came from, in the actor's time zone.
- An email about an approved app, such as one sent while someone signs in to it, is headed by that
  app's logo and name. Every other email is headed by the tenant. An app nobody approved never heads
  an email, so a self-registered app cannot use the tenant's mail to pass as someone else.

To preview every email masks sends, open **Settings**, then **Messages**, then **Templates** in
`/manage`. Each preview uses sample actors and the tenant's own name and links.

### Editing an email template

A manager holding `masks:manage` can edit these emails on the same page:

- invitation
- organization invitation
- password reset
- email confirmation
- confirmation code
- approval request, sent to managers
- request for help, sent to managers
- approval

They can also add **Closing lines on every email**.

- The **Subject** (up to 150 characters) and the **Opening text** (up to 2,000 characters) replace
  the ones masks writes. Leave either blank to keep masks' own.
- Both are plain text. Markup shows as written, and no link can be added. A blank line starts a new
  paragraph.
- `{{tenant}}`, `{{name}}`, `{{nickname}}`, `{{organization}}`, `{{role}}`, and `{{code}}` are
  placeholders. The page lists which ones each email offers. A placeholder an email does not offer
  is refused.
- masks still adds the button or the code, how long it lasts, and the lines that tell an actor what
  to do if it was not them. A password reset that a manager started still names the manager.
- A template applies in every language the tenant serves.
- masks records each change as `mail_template.updated`.

## Keeping and exporting activity

masks keeps each event for 180 days by default. A manager holding `masks:manage` changes this under
**Settings**, then **General**, then **Activity**, from 30 days to seven years. Older events are
deleted each night, so a shorter period takes effect the next night.

To download a copy:

1. Open **Settings**, then **Activity**.
2. Choose a range of up to 366 days under **Export**.
3. Choose **Download**.

About the file:

- It has one event per line, as JSON, in the same shape that
  [event streams](/build/event-streams/#what-is-sent) send.
- It follows the filter on the page.
- Any manage role may download it. masks records each download as `events.exported`.
- The link lasts ten minutes. It works only in a browser signed in as the manager who asked for it.
- A range with more than 250,000 events is refused.

For a copy that keeps up to date on its own, use an [event stream](/build/event-streams/).

## Calls to other servers

masks calls addresses that apps and managers supply. A bad address could make masks call a server
on a private network, so masks checks each one. The calls are:

- a client's keys, sector identifier, logo, metadata document, back-channel logout, SAML single
  logout, and shared signals endpoint
- a resource's protected resource metadata
- every provider's endpoints and SAML metadata
- each mail and SMS service
- each event stream's endpoint
- the Pwned Passwords API

For each call, masks:

- looks up the hostname, and refuses it if any of its addresses is private, loopback, link-local, or
  reserved
- connects to the address it checked, for every call except mail
- stops at a time limit and a size limit

In development and test, masks allows `http` and private addresses.

Some apps and providers live on a private network, such as a tailnet (a private network across your
devices) or an identity provider inside the office. List their address ranges in
[`MASKS_OUTBOUND_ALLOWED`](/reference/environment/#outbound-calls).

:::caution
Every client that can register itself can make masks call a range in `MASKS_OUTBOUND_ALLOWED`. List
only the ranges you mean.
:::

## Rotating signing keys

masks publishes a new key before it signs anything with it. Clients that cache the keys then have
the new key before they see a token it signed. See
[signing keys](/build/core-concepts/#signing-keys) for the states a key moves through.

Managers holding `masks:manage:security` or `masks:manage` rotate keys under **Settings**, then
**General**, then **Signing keys**.

| Action | Does | The outgoing key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Stage** | Publishes a new key ahead of time. One at a time. | Keeps signing. |
| **Activate** | Makes the staged key the signing key. | Verifies for 24 hours. |
| **Rotate now** | Makes a key and signs with it at once. Use it when caches cannot wait. | Verifies for 24 hours. |
| **Discard** | Removes a staged key, which has signed nothing. | Keeps signing. |

SAML applications must read masks' metadata again after a key is staged, and before it is
activated.

### Rotating on a schedule

A new tenant rotates its keys every 90 days. A manager holding `masks:manage` changes **Rotation**
to every 30, 180, or 365 days, or to **By hand**. A tenant set up before masks-server 0.13 is still
**By hand**, and the health panel says so until a manager picks a schedule. A daily job then:

1. Stages the next key a day before the active key reaches that age.
2. Activates a key once it has been staged for a day.

With a schedule set, a key staged by hand is also activated a day after it is staged. The job
records each step in the activity.

## Where a sign-in error goes

A bad `/authorize` link ends with an error. Where masks sends that error depends on who registered
the client.

- An [approved client](/build/features/#registering-a-client) hears the error at its `redirect_uri`,
  with `error`, `error_description`, `state`, and `iss`, as OAuth describes.
- A self-registered client's errors show on a page on masks. The person stays on masks and reads
  what went wrong. Nothing is sent to the client's `redirect_uri`.

This covers errors masks finds in the request, such as a scope the client does not hold, an
unsupported `response_type`, or a request object that fails a rule, and sign-ins masks refuses, such
as a suspended account, a group the person is not in, or a consent the person declined.

Two answers go back to the `redirect_uri` whoever registered the client, because OpenID Connect
requires them: `interaction_required` for a `prompt=none` request that needs the person, and a
`redirect_uri` on masks' own origin.

Registration is open by default, so anyone can register a client with a `redirect_uri` of their own.
Without this rule, a link that starts at masks could bounce a person to any site with one bad
parameter.

## Pushed requests

A normal authorization request puts every parameter in the address bar. There, browser history,
logs, and later pages can read it.

A pushed request ([RFC 9126](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9126.html)) sends the parameters
from the client's server straight to `/par`. Only a reference goes in the URL. Discovery advertises
`pushed_authorization_request_endpoint`.

1. Post the parameters to `/par`. Authenticate the same way as at `/token`. Include `client_id` in
   the body, even with Basic auth. A public client sends its `client_id` and no secret.

   ```sh
   curl -u "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" https://demo.auth.example.com/par \
     -d client_id="$CLIENT_ID" \
     -d response_type=code \
     -d redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/cb \
     -d scope="openid profile" \
     -d code_challenge="$CHALLENGE" \
     -d code_challenge_method=S256 \
     -d state="$STATE"
   ```

   ```json
   {
     "request_uri": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:8mZ1...",
     "expires_in": 90
   }
   ```

2. Redirect to `/authorize` with only the client ID and the reference:

   ```
   https://demo.auth.example.com/authorize
     ?client_id=...
     &request_uri=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Arequest_uri%3A8mZ1...
   ```

The reference lasts 90 seconds, works once, and works only for the client that pushed it. Following
it twice, late, or with another `client_id` returns `invalid_request_uri`.

### Requiring pushed requests

:::caution
Turn this on only after the client already pushes its requests.
:::

```graphql
mutation {
  updateClient(clientId: "...", requirePushedAuthorizationRequests: true) {
    client {
      clientId
    }
  }
}
```

After this, masks refuses a plain `/authorize` link for that client with `invalid_request`. A
self-registered client can ask for the same setting when it registers.

## Signed requests

A client with `jwks` or a `jwks_uri` can send the whole request as a signed JWT, a JSON token with a
signature. This is called a request object ([RFC 9101](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9101.html)),
and it holds the parameters as claims:

```json
{
  "iss": "$CLIENT_ID",
  "aud": "https://demo.auth.example.com",
  "client_id": "$CLIENT_ID",
  "exp": 1789000300,
  "nbf": 1789000000,
  "jti": "5c1f...",
  "response_type": "code",
  "redirect_uri": "https://app.example.com/cb",
  "scope": "openid profile",
  "code_challenge": "$CHALLENGE",
  "code_challenge_method": "S256",
  "state": "$STATE"
}
```

Send it as `request`, next to `client_id`, to `/authorize` or `/par`.

| Claim or property | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `typ` | `oauth-authz-req+jwt`, `application/oauth-authz-req+jwt`, `jwt`, or none. |
| Signature | RSA, RSA-PSS, or ECDSA, with a registered key. `none` and shared secrets are refused. |
| `iss` | The client. |
| `aud` | This issuer. |
| `client_id` | The same as the `client_id` next to it. |
| `exp` | Required. At most an hour away. |
| `nbf` | Optional. Not in the future, and at most an hour ago. |
| `jti` | Optional. Used up on first use. |

- A pushed request or a request object is the whole request. masks ignores anything else in the
  `/authorize` query.
- masks refuses a request object with `invalid_request_object` if it fails a rule, or if it holds
  its own `request` or `request_uri`.
- `requireSignedRequestObject` on `updateClient` requires signing, in the same way that
  `requirePushedAuthorizationRequests` requires pushing.
- masks accepts only a `request_uri` it issued from `/par`. It never fetches one from a client URL.
- A key set read from a `jwks_uri` is kept for five minutes. A key id masks has not seen makes it
  read the set again, at most once in those five minutes, so a stranger cannot make masks fetch an
  app's keys over and over.

## Binding a token with DPoP

A bearer token works for anyone who holds it. DPoP ([RFC 9449](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449))
binds a token to a key the client keeps. A copied token is then useless without the key. masks binds
a token for any client that asks.

1. The client generates a key pair and keeps it.
2. For each request, it signs a _proof_. A proof is a JWT typed `dpop+jwt` that names the method and
   URL, with the public key in its header.
3. It sends the proof in the `DPoP` header:

   ```
   POST /token HTTP/1.1
   DPoP: eyJ0eXAiOiJkcG9wK2p3dCIsImFsZyI6IkVTMjU2Iiwiandr...
   ```

4. masks returns a bound token:

   ```json
   { "access_token": "...", "token_type": "DPoP", "expires_in": 3600 }
   ```

The token's `cnf` claim holds `jkt`, the key's SHA-256 thumbprint
([RFC 7638](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7638)). A thumbprint is a short hash that identifies
the key.

To use the token, the client:

- sends it with the `DPoP` scheme
- sends a new proof every time
- includes `ath`, the token's hash, in each proof sent with a token

```
GET /userinfo HTTP/1.1
Authorization: DPoP eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...
DPoP: eyJ0eXAiOiJkcG9wK2p3dCIs...
```

### What masks refuses

- a bound token sent as `Bearer`
- a proof whose `htm` or `htu` names another request
- a proof with no `ath`, or the wrong one
- a proof older than 90 seconds, or more than 30 seconds in the future
- a proof with no `jti`, or one already seen
- a proof that holds a private key, a symmetric key, or `alg: none`
- any algorithm except `ES256`, `ES384`, `ES512`, `PS256`, `PS384`, `PS512`, and `RS256`

A refused proof returns:

- at a resource, `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP error="invalid_dpop_proof"` and the accepted
  `algs`
- at `/token`, `400 invalid_dpop_proof`

At a resource, a bound token with a valid proof made by another key returns `401` with
`error="invalid_token"`.

masks sends no nonce.

### Binding earlier

- **Authorization code.** `dpop_jkt` on `/authorize` binds the code to the key, so an intercepted
  code cannot be redeemed:

  ```
  GET /authorize?...&dpop_jkt=NzbLsXh8uDCcd-6MNwXF4W_7noWXFZAfHkxZsRGC9Xs
  ```

- **Refresh token.** A bound grant's refresh token is bound too. masks refuses a proof that does not
  match before it uses up the refresh token.

### Requiring a bound token

masks refuses a token without a proof to a client with `dpop_bound_access_tokens` set.

- A client sets it when it registers.
- A manager sets it with `dpopBoundAccessTokens` on `updateClient`.

```json
{ "client_name": "...", "dpop_bound_access_tokens": true }
```

## Rich authorization requests

A scope says what kind of thing an app may do. `authorization_details`
([RFC 9396](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9396)) says exactly what. For example, one payment of
123.50 euros to one payee.

### Declaring a type

An approved client that serves these requests declares each type it accepts. It does this under
**Authorization details** on its **Endpoints** tab in `/manage`, in **Types it accepts**.

A declaration has:

- a label for the consent screen
- a schema
- optionally, `remember`

```json
{
  "payment_initiation": {
    "label": "Send a payment",
    "remember": 2592000,
    "schema": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["instructedAmount"],
      "properties": {
        "instructedAmount": {
          "type": "object",
          "required": ["currency", "amount"],
          "properties": {
            "currency": { "type": "string", "enum": ["EUR", "USD"] },
            "amount": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 20 }
          }
        },
        "creditorName": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 140 }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

- A schema can use `type`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `enum`,
  `maxLength`, `maxItems`, `minimum`, `maximum`, `title`, and `description`.
- A field the schema does not list is refused, unless `additionalProperties` is `true`.
- `remember` is a number of seconds, up to 400 days. Without it, the consent screen asks about the
  type every time.
- Discovery lists every declared type in `authorization_details_types_supported`.

### Asking

The app that asks:

1. Registers the types it uses in `authorization_details_types`, shown as **Types it may ask for**.
2. Sends the details as a JSON array to `/authorize` or `/par`, or in a signed request object.

```
GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=…&scope=openid
  &authorization_details=[{"type":"payment_initiation","instructedAmount":{"currency":"EUR","amount":"123.50"},"creditorName":"Merchant A"}]
```

masks refuses these with `invalid_authorization_details`:

- a type nobody declared
- a type the app did not register
- an entry its schema does not allow
- more than ten entries
- more than 8 kilobytes

`client_credentials` does not accept them.

### Consent

The consent screen lists each entry with its label and fields.

- It asks about every entry, even when the actor allowed the app before.
- It skips an entry only when the actor allowed it before and its type sets `remember`. masks keeps
  that allowed entry on the actor's consent for that long.
- If any entry in a request is not kept, the screen asks about all of them.
- An app that skips consent still asks about entries that are not kept.

The actor sees what is kept, and until when, under **Apps you have let in** on their account page. A
manager sees it on the actor's and the app's consents in `/manage`.

masks forgets a kept entry when the app is revoked, or when the client's
[consent lifetime](/build/features/#consent) ends.

### Tokens

- The granted details are in the token response, the access token's `authorization_details` claim,
  and introspection.
- At the token endpoint, the app can send `authorization_details` to narrow an access token to some
  of the granted entries.
- A refresh token keeps every granted entry.
- A [token exchange](/build/connecting-via-sdk/#exchanging-a-token) passes them on or narrows them.
- Nothing can add an entry that was not granted.
